lead: Networks are sorted by reach and by who pays for the links. A PAN spans a few metres and one person owns it. A LAN spans a room to a campus and one organisation owns every cable and switch. A MAN spans a city and a provider usually runs it. A WAN crosses states or countries on links leased from carriers. Joining two or more networks gives an internetwork; the Internet is the largest. Every design choice depends on which you are building.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for the five parts every network is built from — message, sender, receiver, medium and protocol.

sections.h3: Four sizes, from pocket to planet

blocks.text: Classification is about span first, then ownership. A network inside one owner's budget and legal boundary is a LAN; one crossing public roads, other buildings or national borders is a WAN, whatever its length on a map.

items: PAN — personal area network. A few metres. Phone to Bluetooth earbuds, laptop to wireless mouse. One person owns both ends; no provider; a few Mbps.

LAN — local area network. Room, office floor or campus. One organisation owns cable, switches and Wi-Fi access points. Speed: 100 Mbps to 10 Gbps on copper or fibre. A VLAN is a logical LAN inside one switch; see Unit 3, Ethernet and VLANs.

MAN — metropolitan area network. One city. A provider sells metro Ethernet to offices across Chennai, or a cable operator runs fibre down every street. Span roughly 5 km to 50 km; one provider owns the street-level links.

WAN — wide area network. Between cities, states or countries. A firm rents a 34 Mbps link from an ISP or telecom carrier; the carrier owns the long-distance fibre. Lower speed per rupee than a LAN; the path crosses many provider switches.

Internetwork. Two or more networks joined by routers. Your home LAN plus your ISP's network plus a web server's LAN is already an internetwork. The Internet is the biggest: millions of networks under different owners, all speaking IP.

blocks.text: Span is a rough guide, not a law. Wi-Fi inside one building is a LAN. A 40 km fibre linking two plants of one company is a private WAN-style link though 40 km sounds like a MAN. Ownership and operation settle it.

sections.h3: LAN against WAN, side by side

blocks.text: Every LAN-versus-WAN difference comes from one root: a LAN has one owner, a WAN has several. One owner means one set of standards, short runs and easy upgrades. Several owners mean contracts, tariffs and fixed interfaces.

blocks.text: Cost per bit decides architecture. Moving a terabyte across a LAN costs a few rupees of electricity; across a leased international link it can cost lakhs. So companies keep full backups inside one building and replicate only changed data across the WAN.

sections.h3: Access, core, and the leased-line versus VPN choice

blocks.text: A provider network has two parts. The access network is the link from your building to the provider's first router — home fibre, office Ethernet handoff, a 4G modem. The core is the high-capacity router and fibre mesh between cities. A MAN or WAN is mostly a core plus thousands of access links. The core is shared, so it runs at tens or hundreds of Gbps.
A company with two distant offices has two standard choices.

items: Private WAN link (leased line). The carrier gives a fixed-rate circuit, say 34 Mbps, reserved for your traffic. Delay is steady and errors rare because the circuit is yours. You pay fixed monthly rent whether you use it or not.

VPN over the Internet. You buy ordinary Internet connections at both ends and run an encrypted tunnel between routers. Capacity is whatever the Internet gives at that moment; delay varies; an attacker sees ciphertext but not your data. Far cheaper and set up in hours.

blocks.text: Use a leased line for guaranteed rate and steady delay — voice, machine control, bank clearing. Use a VPN when cost matters more than jitter — file sync, email, remote staff. Many firms run both.

examples.question: A firm has three Chennai offices on a provider's metro Ethernet service and one Dubai office on a 34 Mbps WAN link. (a) Name the network type of the Chennai group, of the Dubai link, and of everything together. (b) Ignoring overhead, how long does a 68 MB file take to Dubai?
steps: Three Chennai offices plus metro Ethernet cover one city under one provider: a MAN.
Chennai-to-Dubai crosses countries on carrier fibre: a WAN.
All pieces joined by routers form one internetwork.
examples.answer: (a) Chennai group: MAN; Dubai link: WAN; together: internetwork. (b) 16 s.

examples.question: A college sends a 250 MB nightly backup to a branch 600 km away. It can rent a 100 Mbps leased line or use a 200 Mbps Internet VPN. Ignoring overhead and delay variation, how long does each take?
steps: The VPN is faster only because its quoted rate is double; its real rate and delay vary.
examples.answer: Leased line: 20 s. VPN: 10 s. The VPN wins on speed here but gives no guarantee.

traps: Judging by distance alone. A 40 km link inside one company is private WAN-style; Wi-Fi in one building is a LAN.
Mixing MB and Mbit. 68 MB is 544 Mbit, eight times bigger. Dividing by 8 wrongly puts you off by 64.
Calling a VPN a private line. A VPN rides the public Internet, so rate and delay are shared; encryption hides content, not congestion.
Assuming a MAN always belongs to an ISP. A company can lease dark fibre across a city, so classify by span and operation together.
Confusing an internetwork with the Internet. Any two joined networks are an internetwork; the Internet is only the largest.

quiz.q: Define a LAN and give typical span and speed.
quiz.a: A LAN covers a room to a campus, is owned by one organisation, and runs at 100 Mbps to 10 Gbps on private cable or Wi-Fi.
Two or more networks joined by routers so hosts on one can reach hosts on another. The Internet is the largest.

quiz.q: Why is WAN error rate higher than LAN?
quiz.a: A WAN runs long distances, crosses many provider switches and public rights of way, and shares links with other customers. Longer cable, more equipment and more interference raise wrong-bit chance.

quiz.q: Why does cost per bit decide where backups are kept?
quiz.a: LAN cost per bit is tiny; a WAN link is rented monthly at a fixed rate. Sending a full terabyte over WAN wastes rent, so companies keep full backups locally and send only changed data.

quiz.q: A 100 MB file is sent over a 50 Mbps link. Ignoring overhead, how long?
Classify each: (i) Bluetooth earbuds to a phone, (ii) an office floor of 40 PCs on one switch, (iii) a cable TV operator's fibre across one city, (iv) an Indian bank's link to its London branch.
quiz.a: (i) PAN, a few metres. (ii) LAN, one owner, one building. (iii) MAN, one city, provider owned. (iv) WAN, crosses countries on a carrier link.

quiz.q: A hospital must send scans to a lab 30 km away and cannot tolerate variable delay. Compare a leased line and a VPN.
quiz.a: A leased line gives fixed rate and steady delay because the circuit is reserved; scans arrive predictably; cost is fixed monthly rent. A VPN is cheaper and quicker to set up but shares Internet capacity, so delay and rate vary at peak hours. Because steady delay is needed, the leased line is right, possibly with VPN backup.

quiz.q: A firm says its network is a WAN because the cable is 25 km long. Is that correct?
quiz.a: Not necessarily. Span alone does not decide. If one company owns and operates all 25 km of fibre between its own buildings, it behaves like a private WAN-style link inside one owner's boundary. If rented from a carrier across a city, it is a MAN; if it crosses into another state, it is a WAN. Ownership and operation count as much as distance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Software-defined WAN lets one controller steer traffic over broadband, 4G and MPLS and pick the cheapest path meeting each application's delay target. Metro Ethernet and carrier MPLS still carry most enterprise traffic between cities; 5G fixed wireless competes with fibre for access.
